prompt: Each moment below belongs to one stage of consumption. Sort them into Prepurchase, Purchase and Postpurchase.

cards.text: A runner notices her shoes are worn out and reads reviews of new ones.
cards.explanation: In prepurchase the consumer identifies a need and searches for information.

cards.text: A juice brand asks shoppers how they feel about its new bottle before launch.
cards.explanation: In prepurchase the marketer studies how consumer attitudes form.

cards.text: A shopper gives up because the website's checkout page keeps crashing.
cards.explanation: In the purchase stage the consumer experiences the store, website, and checkout.

cards.text: A bookstore changes its lighting and music to make browsing feel calmer.
cards.explanation: In the purchase stage the marketer focuses on packaging, convenience, and store atmosphere.

cards.text: After a week of use, a buyer decides his new headphones feel cheap.
cards.explanation: In postpurchase the consumer uses the product and judges its quality.

cards.text: A coffee-machine brand counts how many machines come back and how many buyers reorder pods.
cards.explanation: In postpurchase the marketer monitors satisfaction, returns, and repeat purchases.

prompt: Which of these shoppers fits the old economic model, and which behaves like a real person? Sort them into the two groups.

cards.text: Reads the label of every cereal on the shelf before choosing one.
cards.explanation: The old model assumed buyers compare all choices.

cards.text: Works out the full cost of every phone plan, then picks the cheapest overall.
cards.explanation: The old model assumed buyers calculate costs and pick the best option.

cards.text: Grabs the same toothpaste as always without looking at the others.
cards.explanation: Habits and brand loyalty act as a mental shortcut.

cards.text: Buys a cake after a bad day at work.
Buys the sneakers everyone in her friend group is wearing.
cards.explanation: Real decisions depend on social pressure.

cards.text: Tired after a long shift, takes the first familiar pasta sauce he sees.
cards.explanation: Real people have limited time and energy, so they use mental shortcuts instead.

prompt: Match each segmentation base with the company that is using it.

pairs.match: A bank designs an account for students under 25.
pairs.explanation: Demographics group people by age, gender, income, and education.

pairs.match: A ski shop sends one offer to snowy cities and another to warm coastal cities.
pairs.explanation: Geographics group people by location, city size, and climate.

pairs.match: A clothing brand targets people who value an outdoor, eco-friendly lifestyle.
pairs.explanation: Psychographics group people by lifestyle, values, and personality.

pairs.match: A café rewards the customers who come in every single day.
pairs.explanation: Behavioral segments group people by how often they buy and how they use the item.
